documents.title: Arbitration Procedures for Compensation Discrimination Claims (Guild/The Washington Post)
documents.subject: Established procedures for resolving individual claims of discrimination in wages/compensation based on gender, race, and/or Hispanic origin between the Guild and The Washington Post; claims window starting September 1, 1994; claims delivered to Carol McNamee, Vice President Government Affairs
documents.date: 1994 (period referenced: from September 1, 1994 to the Negotiated Settlement Agreement)
documents.notes: Single typewritten page photographed rotated 90 degrees (text runs vertically). Stamped/typed heading 'ARBITRATION PROCEDURES'. Page ends mid-sentence after the addressee line, so more pages of this exhibit exist elsewhere. Date figures (1994) read consistently but the document belongs to the settlement-era arbitration framework, so a human may wish to verify against the batch 2002/2003 documents.

pages.transcript:
[Image rotated 90 degrees.] ARBITRATION PROCEDURES

These procedures are established for the resolution of certain individual claims of discrimination on the basis of gender, race (i.e., Black, White, Asian, Native American), and/or Hispanic origin in wages or other compensation in Guild-covered positions. Claims may be asserted by current employees who occupy Guild-covered positions or who have occupied Guild-covered positions at any time between September 1, 1994 and the date of the Negotiated Settlement Agreement. Claims shall be limited to claims of discrimination in compensation on the basis of gender, race, and/or Hispanic origin after August 31, 1994. Such claims shall not be barred on the ground that the initial act of discrimination occurred before September 1, 1994. In all cases, however, relief shall be limited to the period beginning September 1, 1994. Claims shall be limited to compensation claims and shall not include claims based on allegedly discriminatory promotions, transfers, assignments or other matters that might affect compensation. Filing a claim under these procedures will waive any right the employee otherwise might have to file the claim in any agency or court.

Claims will be heard by an arbitrator agreed upon by the Guild and the Post, and shall be subject to the following procedures:

1. Claims must be made in writing on a claim form that is available from the Personnel Department or the Guild. Claim forms must be delivered, or postmarked for delivery, to Carol McNamee, Vice President Government Affairs, The Washington Post, [text continues on next page, not photographed]

documents.title: Personal Statement / Declaration of Grievant (page 8; paragraphs 26-28)
documents.subject: First-person numbered statement describing the writer's career at The Washington Post: 1993 transfer to the local news beat (approved by Financial AME David Ignatius), 1994 shift to general assignments, Latin America 1994 investment-boom coverage, and the 1994 Associated Press Mark Twain Award for extreme-cold coverage. Content is consistent with Martha M. Hamilton's own account; attribution inferred, not stated on the page.
documents.notes: Single page (typed with a monospace typewriter face, unlike DOC-001), carries printed page number '- 8 -' and continues a sentence from the prior page. Includes footnote 4 on beats and front-page visibility.

pages.transcript:
meeting included the women's concerns about beats, stories, money and attitude.

26. In 1993, in part because of some serious family and personal problems and my need to be closer to home, I asked to cover local news. Financial AME David Ignatius approved my taking over the beat. I did a good job on the beat despite an extremely difficult personal situation which became increasingly complicated. I put together a focus group of area business leaders which resulted in an article that I wrote along with our polling director Rich Morin that elicited a note from Don Graham who referred to it as an "excellent article."

27. In 1994, I shifted to general assignments4 because I was concerned that my personal and family circumstances made it hard for me to cover a beat. I didn't want the newspaper to miss stories on a beat because I was called to a family emergency. But I also did important and high profile work for the Post during this period. For instance, the Financial section sent me to Latin America to cover the 1994 investment boom there. In my evaluation I was described as a "superior reporter" wit [sic] "a keen eye for offbeat but fascinating subjects" who is "skillful in explaining complicated stories."

28. In 1994, I received the Associated Press Mark Twain Award for coverage of the extreme cold snap that year. Although I was not an energy reporter at the time, I contributed to our coverage of how the utilities responded.

__________

4 Without a beat, it can be harder to develop high profile stories, and often GA reporters are called on to write secondary stories on someone else's beat while the beat reporter covers the higher profile story. When it comes to beats, many beats are high profile by their very nature—e.g., covering the markets and Wall Street or the Federal Reserve Board or the national economy lead to more front page stories than others.

documents.title: Letter from Black female reporters of The Washington Post to 'Leonard' on salary disparities
documents.subject: Signed-style letter from Black women working at The Washington Post to a recipient named Leonard, citing Don Graham's radio statement that the average Post reporter earns $50,000/year, the Guild's salary-differences report (Black female reporters averaging $791.33/week vs. $986.68 white males, $920.46 black males, $859.37 white females), and the resulting $10,262.20/year gap between black women and white males
documents.date: Jan. 2, 1967 (as typed; note context — Guild salary report and WDOL-AM/Don Graham reference — may suggest the year is actually 1987 or 1997; verify)
documents.notes: Single page on Washington Post letterhead (1150 15th Street, N.W.). The typed date visually reads 'Jan. 2, 1967'; flagged because the internal content (salary levels) appears anomalous for 1967 — possibly a mistyped date or my misreading of one digit; set confidence medium. Letter appears to continue (no signature block visible on this sheet). Radio station reads 'WDOL-AM' as typed.

pages.transcript:
The Washington Post
1150 15TH STREET, N.W.
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20071
(202) 334-6000

WRITER'S DIRECT TELEPHONE NUMBER [blank]

Jan. 2, 1967

Dear Leonard:

As black women working at the Washington Post, we are deeply concerned about the disparities between our salaries and those of our colleagues.

During a recent WDOL-AM radio show, Don Graham stated that the average salary for a Washington Post reporter is $50,000 per year. As far as we can determine, only two of 17 black females in the newsroom receive salaries at or above that level.

As you are aware, the Guild's report on salary differences found that black female reporters receive an average of $791.33 per week compared to averages of $986.68 for white males, $920.46 for black males and $859.37 for white females.

While we are concerned about the salary gaps that such statistics reveal between white males and all other employees and between men and women, we wish to address the salary levels of black women because clearly we are at the bottom.

Graham's statement about average salaries coupled with the Guild report has made it clear that black women are the least valued employees in the newsroom. At least five earn less than the $791.33 weekly average. We are also concerned that the merit system is not applied in an evenhanded manner.

As Post employees, we feel that we are not being treated fairly. Whether our salaries are part of a pattern of discrimination, as the Guild maintained in its report, or the unintended impact of a dual tier pay system, the result is the same. Black women are the lowest paid in the newsroom. Using the average weekly salaries, the gap between black women and white males, for example, is $10,262.20 a year.

documents.title: Confidential settlement submission: comparator analyses — Pearlstein and Mark Potts (vs. Hamilton)
documents.subject: Header-marked confidential arbitration/settlement material comparing the Post careers and salaries of Michael Pearlstein and Mark Potts to Martha Hamilton's: Pearlstein's seven merit increases (1994-2002), high starting salary vs. Walsh, fast-track status; Potts's higher pay in the 1992 and 1993 salary snapshots, his experience/education, and starting salary relative to Hamilton and Mayer
documents.notes: Single typed (proportional-font typescript, matching DOC-001's era) page with all-caps header 'CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES / PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES'. Internally notes seven merit increases but lists five years (1994, 1996, 1997, 2001, 2002) — transcribed exactly as seen.

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

As of September 1, 2002, Pearlstein had received seven merit increases – all of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these merit increases in the following years: 1994, 1996, 1997, 2001 and 2002.

Explanation:
Pearlstein was paid a high salary by his previous employer – more than the salary of Walsh at The Post at that time. Therefore, his starting salary at The Post was substantially more than the salary of Walsh at that time.

Pearlstein joined The Post as a Deputy Editor in Financial News – a position of great responsibility. He retained his editor's salary when he became a reporter in Financial News.

Pearlstein covers issues involving the national economy – an important and challenging position in Financial News – and is able to synthesize weighty and complex economic issues into readable and understandable articles.

Pearlstein is highly valued in the marketplace – one of the individuals in Financial News whom The Post could ill afford to lose. As a result, Pearlstein was put on the fast-track.

Pearlstein was the chief architect of The Post's Sunday Financial Section, for which he writes and edits two pages.

Mark Potts

Mark Potts was paid more than Hamilton on the 1992 and 1993 salary snapshots. Potts and Mayer did not work together in Financial News at that time

Experience and Education
Potts came to The Post in the early 1980s as a reporter in Financial News. He became the Assignment Editor in Financial News in 1987, returning to Financial News as a reporter in 1989. Potts left The Post in 1993. Prior to starting at The Post, Potts worked as a reporter at The Chicago Tribune for approximately two and-a-half years. He also worked as a reporter at The Associated Press for approximately one-and-a-half years and as a part-time copy aide at The Washington Post for nine months. Potts is a graduate of George Washington University.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Potts received approximately a five percent increase over his prior salary at the Chicago Tribune. His starting salary was less than the salary of Hamilton at that time and slightly more than the salary of Mayer at that time.
